description: 'Ships and closes an approved work item (pull request, merge, sandbox or production deployment, requirements update, Done), or cancels an item with the owner''s reason. Use when the owner says "ship it", "deploy it", "close it out", or "mark it done", or asks to cancel or drop an item.'

# Work finish

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Takes an approved item through the pull request, merge, deployment, and requirements update to Done, or cancels it; it never marks Done without the owner's approval and never runs a production deploy. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Check the result approval is recorded. Not recorded: show the result, the gaps, and the evidence, and ask. "Ship it" or "mark it done" after he saw the result counts: save his words first, then record it (`references/approvals.md`, section 4). Each sub-item needs its own.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Result approved; work-finish continues.'`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
2. Repository work: commit the item's files by name on its branch, push it, open the pull request, and set the stage (`references/closing.md`, section 2; `references/git-rules.md` before any Git write).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 12-pr-and-push`
3. Merge through `merge-and-clean-up` only with the owner's yes to this merge, or a standing merge instruction with an independent check on the exact head (`references/closing.md`, section 3). No remote: the local merge (`references/closing.md`, section 4), then this note.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'No remote: merged locally into <default branch>.' --effect 'No pull request; no deployment.'`
4. Deployment, when the item needs one (`references/closing.md`, section 5). Production deploys and production data loads are the owner's to run. Salesforce: a sandbox validate runs; a sandbox deploy needs his yes for that deploy, and in Codex he runs every sandbox deploy and sandbox data change himself, so give him the exact command with its `-o <sandbox>`. Run each `sf` command directly, never from a script.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 13-deployment`
5. Requirements baseline: copy only delivered and approved behavior into the area's file in `requirements/`, update `system-guide/` when the structure changed, and save both with `publish-docs` (`references/closing.md`, section 6).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 14-spec-update`
6. Sub-items: list the open ones; each is finished, cancelled, or moved on its own (`references/closing.md`, section 7).
   `toolkit work list --tree`
7. Memory: at most one `event` record through `memory-save`, only when the episode will matter later.
8. Before Done, run the Done checklist in `references/approvals.md`, section 5, with the Overview and Roadmap updates and the leftover worktrees in `references/closing.md`, sections 9 and 10. Then mark it Done. The command also backs up the tracker and memory: read its backup line. "No backup folder is set" or a line with "failed" goes to the owner as a question (`references/closing.md`, section 10).
   `toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>'`
9. Take the item off the current focus (`references/current-focus.md`). Say whether the work reached the default branch. End with the one question (the merge, the deploy, a leftover branch, the backup folder) or "Tell me the next thing to build."
10. Cancel instead: the owner's words are the reason; ask about each open sub-item first (`references/approvals.md`, section 6).
    `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Never mark Done without a recorded result approval or the owner's quoted words. The CLI needs `--by`, and `--quote` when no result approval is recorded.
- Never mark Done while the item's changes, or its `requirements/` and `system-guide/` updates, are uncommitted.
- A result approval never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing. Each needs the owner's yes or a standing instruction recorded in `DECISIONS.md`.
- A standing merge instruction needs an `acceptance-checker` that did not build the change to find no blocking issue on that exact head. Without that check, ask the owner.
- Agents never run a production deploy or a production data load. Hand the owner the exact command and what to check afterwards; record his report in a history note.
- In Codex, every Git write needs the owner's approval and escalated permissions (`references/git-rules.md`). No remote: never run `git fetch` or `git push`.
- No AI credit in commits, pull requests, or release notes. The pull request description goes through `unslop`.
- Stages that do not apply are skipped, each with one history note saying so.
- Leave the folder or card where it is. Moving or archiving is `work-organize`'s, on the owner's request.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Close the issue as completed, or as not planned for a cancel (`references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`).

## Agents

- `acceptance-checker` (`references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`): the independent check of the exact head before a merge under a standing merge instruction. Brief it as `work-check` does and name the commit (`references/helpers.md`).
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Give the full text of this skill's `references/agent-<name>.md`, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran. Without an independent check, a standing merge instruction does not apply: ask the owner.

name: merge-and-clean-up
description: 'Merges one approved GitHub pull request and removes only that pull request''s branches and worktree, after its checks and the merge-safety check pass. Use when the owner or work-finish asks to merge a named pull request, for example "merge PR 12", "merge and clean up", or "land this pull request".'
---

# Merge and clean up

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Land one exact pull request, prove it merged, then remove only the workspace
that belonged to it. Merge and cleanup are one guarded workflow.

1. **Resolve the exact pull request** and map branches to worktrees. The local
   head branch must be at the pull request's head commit.
2. **Check the merge is allowed:** the owner's yes for this pull request, or a
   standing merge instruction recorded in `DECISIONS.md`.
3. **Preflight on GitHub:** open, not a draft, mergeable, reviews satisfied,
   required checks passed. "No checks reported" is not a failure.
4. **Merge-safety check:** after a fetch, compare
   `git diff --name-only origin/<default>...<branch>` with `git status` in the
   primary checkout. A file in both lists: stop and name it.
5. **Merge** with
   `gh pr merge <n> --squash --delete-branch --match-head-commit <headRefOid>`,
   using the head commit recorded in step 1 (no admin flags), then confirm the
   state is `MERGED`.
6. **Fast-forward the base checkout**, then remove only this pull request's
   worktree and branches.
7. **Add one history note** to the linked work item. Stage moves and Done stay
   with `work-finish`. Report the link, the merge commit, and the cleanup
   result.

## Gotchas

- Codex keeps `.git/` read-only and turns the network off. Every Git write
  here (`git fetch`, `git pull`, `git push`, `git worktree remove`,
  `git branch -d`) and every `gh` call runs alone, with `sandbox_permissions`
  set to `require_escalated` and a one-line reason. Refused without asking:
  show the owner the exact command and wait (`references/git-rules.md`, "Git
  writes in Codex").
- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): there is no pull request, so this
  skill does not apply. Never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch
  refusal as a blocker. Say so in one line; the local merge of a work item's
  branch belongs to `work-finish` (`references/git-rules.md`, "A project with
  no remote").
- A squash merge leaves the old branch commit outside the base, so
  `git branch -d` can refuse after a good merge. `git branch -D` is allowed
  only for this pull request's head branch, with all five proofs in step 6.
- The result approval of a work item never covers the merge. The merge needs
  its own yes, or a standing merge instruction whose conditions hold on this
  exact head.
- A commit pushed after step 1 would be merged without anyone checking it.
  `--match-head-commit <headRefOid>` makes GitHub refuse the merge when the
  head is no longer the commit step 1 recorded. A refusal means a new commit
  arrived: stop, and run steps 1 to 4 again on the new head.

## Safety rules

- "Merge and clean up" is merge approval only when the target pull request is
  clear from a number, a URL, or the current branch. Ask when more than one
  could match.
- Read the project's `AGENTS.md` and `.claude/rules/` first. Project rules decide
  required checks, merge method, and who may merge.
- Never merge a draft, bypass branch protection, use an admin override,
  force-push, or ignore a failed required check.
- Never delete anything before GitHub reports the pull request as `MERGED`.
- Never delete the default branch, the base branch, an unrelated branch or
  worktree, a dirty worktree, or a branch with local commits that are not in the
  pull request head.
- List every worktree before and after cleanup. Unrelated ones stay.
- If any proof is missing, stop at the safe point and report exactly what
  remains.

## 1. Resolve the exact target

Take the repository and pull request from the number or URL. For "this PR",
resolve it from the current checkout:

```bash
git status -sb
git remote -v
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
gh pr view --json number,url,state,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefName,isCrossRepository,title,body
```

Record: repository owner and name, pull request number and URL, head branch and
head commit, base branch, the worktree holding the head branch (if any), the
worktree holding the base branch, and whether the head branch is in a fork. Map
branches to paths with:

```bash
git worktree list --porcelain
```

If the local head branch exists, its commit must equal `headRefOid` before you
promise it can be deleted. A different commit means local-only work exists: stop
and keep it.

Find the linked work item id: a head branch named like `claude/wi-007-<slug>`
(or `wi-007-<slug>`), or any branch containing `WI-007`, belongs to `WI-007`.
The id prefix is in lower case in a branch name, so `claude/tv2-007-<slug>`
belongs to `TV2-007`. Otherwise look for an id in the pull request title or
body. No id found: skip the history note in step 7.

## 2. Check the merge is allowed

The merge needs one of these:

- The owner's own yes for this pull request, in this conversation.
- A standing merge instruction recorded in `DECISIONS.md` whose conditions
  hold on this exact head. Open `references/approvals.md`, "Standing merge
  instruction", for where it is recorded, the conditions it carries (for
  example an independent check with no blocking findings on this head), and
  what overrides it.

A work item that says its merge needs the owner's approval overrides a
standing instruction. When neither is present, stop and ask the owner.
`work-finish` asks for this approval; this skill only checks it.

## 3. Preflight

```bash
gh pr view <number> --repo <owner/repo> \
  --json number,title,state,isDraft,mergeable,mergeStateStatus,reviewDecision,statusCheckRollup,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefName,isCrossRepository,url
gh pr checks <number> --repo <owner/repo>
```

Merge only when the pull request is open and not a draft, GitHub reports it
mergeable, required reviews are satisfied, required checks passed, and the head
and base still match what step 1 recorded.

- Already merged: skip the merge, record its merge commit, and recheck that the
  head branch and commit match the workspace you plan to remove.
- Closed without merging: stop.
- `gh pr checks` exits nonzero when no checks exist. That means no configured
  check, not a failed one. Run any required local checks the project names, and
  say plainly when no automated check exists.
- Pending checks: wait only when the owner asked you to finish the merge.
- Failed checks: stop and report. Do not merge around them.

The head worktree must be clean before merging:

```bash
git -C <head-worktree> status --porcelain
```

Any output blocks cleanup. Do not stash or discard it.

## 4. Merge-safety check

Other sessions may have uncommitted work in the primary checkout. A merge that
changes the same files would collide with it. The primary checkout is the first
entry that `git worktree list` prints. Fetch first, so the comparison uses the
remote's default branch, not a local copy that may be behind:

```bash
git worktree list
git fetch origin
git diff --name-only origin/<default-branch>...<head-branch>
git -C <primary-checkout> status --porcelain
```

With no local head branch, use `origin/<head-branch>` in the diff. If any file
appears in both lists, stop. Name exactly those files and let the
owner decide whether to commit, stash, or wait. Do not touch the primary
checkout's changes.

## 5. Merge

Use the merge method the owner or the project requires. When neither says:
squash for a normal single-purpose branch; a merge commit when the commit
structure matters; ask when the choice would change history in a way that
matters.

```bash
gh pr merge <number> --repo <owner/repo> --squash --delete-branch --match-head-commit <headRefOid>
```

`<headRefOid>` is the head commit recorded in step 1 and checked again in step
3. Never leave `--match-head-commit` out, and never fill it with a newer
commit to get past a refusal. A refusal means someone pushed after the checks:
stop, report the new commit, and run steps 1 to 4 again on it. A standing
merge instruction covers only the head its independent check saw.

Replace `--squash` with the chosen method when needed. Leave out
`--delete-branch` for a pull request from a fork: that branch belongs to the
contributor. Never add an admin or protection-bypass flag. Then verify:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --repo <owner/repo> \
  --json state,mergedAt,mergeCommit,url,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefName,isCrossRepository
```

Do not clean up unless `state` is `MERGED`.

## 6. Update the base checkout, then remove only the merged workspace

The worktree holding the base branch must be clean and on the expected branch:

```bash
git -C <base-worktree> fetch --prune origin
git -C <base-worktree> pull --ff-only
```

If it is dirty, on another branch, or cannot fast-forward, leave it untouched,
do no local cleanup from it, and report the blocker. Never reset, stash,
switch, or rebase it.

Recheck five proofs before removing anything:

1. GitHub reports this exact pull request merged.
2. The branch to remove is the pull request's head branch, not the base or
   default branch.
3. The worktree to remove is clean.
4. The local branch commit still equals the recorded head commit.
5. No other worktree uses that branch.

Run cleanup from the base worktree, never from inside the worktree being
removed:

```bash
git -C <base-worktree> worktree remove <head-worktree>
git -C <base-worktree> branch -d <head-branch>
git -C <base-worktree> worktree prune
```

A squash merge does not make the old branch commit part of the base, so
`git branch -d` can refuse even after a good merge. Use
`git branch -D <head-branch>` only when all five proofs still hold and that is
the only refusal. This is not permission to force-delete any other branch.

If GitHub did not delete the remote branch, delete it only when it is in the
same repository and belongs to this merged pull request:

```bash
git -C <base-worktree> push origin --delete <head-branch>
git -C <base-worktree> fetch --prune origin
```

Never try to delete a contributor's fork branch.

## 7. Work item note and report

When the project has `.toolkit.json` and step 1 found a work item id, add one
history note:

```text
toolkit work history <id> --note 'Merged pull request <number> as <merge commit>'
```

For a GitHub Issues or Jira tracker, `toolkit work` exits with code 3 and
prints the path of that tracker's written instructions; follow them to add the
same note to the issue. Do not change the stage or mark anything Done: that is
`work-finish`'s job, after the owner approves the result. Do not invent a work
item when none exists.

Verify: the pull request is merged; the base checkout matches its upstream and
is clean; the head branch is gone locally and on the remote; its worktree is
gone; every unrelated worktree remains.

End with the pull request link, the merge commit, the final base state, the
cleanup result, and whether the history note was saved ("Not saved" first when
it failed). The last line is the one question for the owner (a remaining
action he must take), or the exact words that continue ("Say 'finish WI-007'
and I'll close the work item.").

## References

| File | Open it when |
| --- | --- |
| `references/approvals.md` | Step 2: the merge rests on a standing merge instruction, not the owner's yes in this conversation |
| `references/git-rules.md` | Before a Git write in Codex, the merge-safety check in full, or a project with no remote |

The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. An unanswered save question is kept as a proposal: the agent does not rely on it, and `work-decide` shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it. The `memory-save` skill says how.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the owner says he is clearing context or ending the session, or asks for a handoff, use the `handoff` skill, whatever the session's length. When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip the offer for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): skip `git fetch`, and never report a fetch failure as a blocker.
- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

# Approvals and gates

The exact steps to ask for and record each owner approval, and what counts as
one. Run each checklist in order; one wrong or missing command leaves the
item in the wrong state.

## Contents

1. What counts as approval
2. Requirements approval
3. Design approval
4. Result approval
5. Done
6. Cancel
7. Delivery offer
8. Project-wide decision
9. Memory proposal
10. Sub-items and approvals
11. Standing merge instruction
12. When an approve command refuses

## 1. What counts as approval

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the gates and these rules. In short:

- Only the owner's explicit words count. Quote them in a history note.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer ("probably B"), silence, or a
  saved draft is not approval.
- An approval covers only what was shown. It never covers merge, deployment,
  spending, or publishing.
- An approval survives later stages. A stage alone does not prove approval:
  check the approval field (`toolkit work show <id>`).
- A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" answers only a yes-or-no question asked
  earlier in this conversation. When none was asked, or the waiting question
  is not a yes-or-no question, show the decision with its choices and your
  recommendation, and record nothing.
- After a yes, save his words first, in a history note that starts with
  `Owner said:`. Then run the gate's commands. A command that refuses then
  never loses his answer, and no later session asks him again.

| The owner says | After this question | It is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Yes, approved." | "Do you approve these requirements?" | The requirements approval |
| "Go with B." | The design options with a recommendation | The choice and approval of Option B |
| "Looks good." | "Do you approve this result?" | The result approval |
| "Looks good." | "Shall I split WI-12 into these three sub-items?" | A yes to the split only, not a result approval |
| "ok" | Nothing was asked in this chat | Not an answer; ask what he wants |
| "Probably A, but let me think." | The design options | Not an answer; the design stays proposed |
| "Ship it." | He has seen the result, gaps, and evidence | The result approval (record it with his words) |

## 2. Requirements approval

Asked by `work-requirements`. `work-decide` records a later answer.

Before asking:

- [ ] The Agreed goal holds real text. The CLI refuses the approval while it
      still holds the template text.
- [ ] The spec check ran (`requirements-analyst`), and its findings were fixed
      or turned into questions.
- [ ] No Open Questions row linked to a requirement is still open. If one is,
      say which and ask it first.

Ask: show the Agreed goal, each requirement in one line, the Acceptance list,
and any open question. Then ask exactly "Do you approve these requirements?"
as the last line, and set the item waiting on the owner.

```text
toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner
```

After his yes, in this order:

- [ ] Save his words first, so no later session asks him again.
      `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Requirements approved.'`
- [ ] Set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and add who approved it and
      when to its Decision record, in one edit of `Active requirements`.
      `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Active requirements' --set-file <file>`
- [ ] Record the approval. It adds its own history row, marks the Open
      Questions rows that asked for it Answered, sets `waiting_on` to `none`,
      and moves an earlier item to stage 03.
      `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
- [ ] Hand the item back to the agent, unless another question for him is
      still open on it.
      `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
- [ ] Check the record.
      `toolkit work validate <id>`
- [ ] Next: a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design`, unless the
      owner agreed to skip the design. Say a skip in the final reply, not in a
      progress line.

Not yet, or a change: the item stays waiting on him. Record the change and
ask again.

A yes that arrives later (`work-decide` records it):

- The Agreed goal still holds the template text: write the goal he was shown
  with the approval question, then record the approval.
  `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Agreed goal' --text '<goal he was shown>'`
- A requirement still has a linked open question: say which one, open
  `work-requirements` for it, and record the approval once it is answered,
  without asking him again.

## 3. Design approval

Asked by `solution-design`. `work-decide` records a later answer.

Before asking:

- [ ] The design is saved as proposed, and the item waits on the owner. Add no
      Open Questions row for the design approval itself: a proposed design is
      already listed as his decision.
      `toolkit work design <id> --set-file <file> --status proposed`
      `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`

Ask: the options in one sentence each, your recommendation and its reason,
what he will see when it is done, the main risks, and the build order. Then
ask him to choose or approve.

After his yes, or his choice of one option, in this order:

- [ ] Save his words first, so no later session asks him again.
      `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Design approved; work-on plans the build.'`
- [ ] Fill "Recommendation and owner decision": Owner decision (who, when,
      where he said it) and Reason for decision (his reason only; never invent
      one).
- [ ] Fill every "Selected design" subsection and the "Build and verification
      plan" (Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks with one row per
      requirement). `work-check` reads those checks.
- [ ] Remove every leftover template prompt. Leave the Design status line as
      it is.
- [ ] Save the design text.
      `toolkit work design <id> --set-file <file>`
- [ ] Record the approval. It adds its own history row. It refuses (exit
      code 2, `design_not_filled`) while "Selected design" still says
      "Pending owner decision" or holds the template prompt: save the filled
      design first, then run it again, without asking him again.
      `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
- [ ] Hand the item back to the agent, unless another question is still open.
      `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
- [ ] Check the record.
      `toolkit work validate <id>`

He wants changes: record them in the design's Notes > Design changes during
the interview, run a fix round for the named changes only, save it as
proposed again, and ask again.

## 4. Result approval

Asked by `work-check` at stage 11.

Before asking:

- [ ] The tests and every acceptance check ran, and an independent checker
      reported, or you say plainly that no independent check ran.
- [ ] The check is recorded in a history note (what was checked, the
      evidence, the gaps).
- [ ] The item is at stage 11 and waits on the owner. Add no Open Questions
      row: stage 11 already lists the result as his decision.
      `toolkit work set <id> --stage 11-user-approval --waiting-on owner`

Ask: what it does now in his terms, how he can see it himself, the evidence,
and the gaps. Then ask exactly "Do you approve this result?" Never hide a gap
to get a yes.

After his yes, in this order:

- [ ] Save his words first.
      `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Result approved; work-finish continues.'`
- [ ] Record the approval.
      `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
- [ ] Hand the item back to the agent.
      `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
- [ ] Open `work-finish`.

A "no": record his words, turn each problem he names into a task or a
requirement change, and continue checking.

## 5. Done

Asked by `work-finish`. Only `toolkit work finish` sets Done.

Before the finish command:

- [ ] The result approval is recorded, or you have the owner's own words
      approving this result to pass with `--quote`.
- [ ] Every change the item made is committed and reached the default branch,
      or the owner said to leave it on the branch.
- [ ] Requirements and system guide updates are saved through `publish-docs`.
- [ ] Every open sub-item is finished, cancelled, or moved, or the owner said
      the parent is done anyway.
- [ ] Every Roadmap phase the item completed says Done.
- [ ] Overview: Related items current, Current position "Done on <date>:
      <evidence>", Blockers "None.".
- [ ] Leftover worktrees and branches for the item are listed and offered for
      removal.

Then run one of these:

```text
toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>'
toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>' --quote '<his exact words>'
toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>' --allow-open-sub-items
```

The second is only for a result approval not yet recorded. The third is only
for a parent the owner said is done while sub-items are still open; quote his
words in a history note. The command sets Next action and Resume here, and
prints what still needs a note.

The finish command also backs up `.work-items/` and `.memory/` (and Hindsight
memory) to the owner's backup folder and prints one line about it. Read that
line:

- "Backed up ... to <folder>": done. Say it in one line in the reply.
- "No backup folder is set ...": ask the owner for a folder outside the
  project, as a question in the reply. After his answer:
  `toolkit config set backup.dir <folder>` (or `none` when he wants no backup).
- A line with "failed" or "Tell the owner": tell him that line as it is. The
  item is still Done; only the backup is missing.

## 6. Cancel

Asked by `work-finish`. Only `toolkit work cancel` sets Cancelled.

- [ ] The reason is the owner's own words, not a summary.
- [ ] Each open sub-item: ask whether to cancel it, move it to the top level,
      or move it under another item. Never cancel them without asking.
- [ ] `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`

Cancelling keeps the record. Nothing is deleted.

## 7. Delivery offer

Only `work-delegate` makes the offer and records the answer. Every other skill
opens `work-delegate` for it. The recorded value:

```text
toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led
toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led
```

A delivery answer never approves requirements, a design, or a result, and
never widens merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.

## 8. Project-wide decision

Recorded by `work-decide` as a row in `DECISIONS.md` at the project root,
then committed through `publish-docs`.

```text
toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner>
toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner> --replaces D-<n>
```

`DECISIONS.md` is append-only. A changed decision is a new row that names the
one it replaces. Any skill that meets a project-wide decision opens
`work-decide`, which runs the full order of work with `publish-docs`.

## 9. Memory proposal

A memory the owner did not answer ("Save to memory?") is saved as a proposal:
status `needs-review`. The agent does not rely on it until he approves it.

```text
toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>
toolkit memory reject <key>
```

A rejection deletes the proposal. Never propose the same fact again in other
words.

## 10. Sub-items and approvals

- A child made with `--covers R-02,R-03` links those parent requirements and
  inherits the parent's requirements approval. The owner is never asked to
  approve the same requirement twice.
- A parent design the owner approved covers its `--covers` children: they
  start at planning (stage 06) with no design of their own.
- A child that needs new behavior gets its own `R-xx` and its own approval.
- Each sub-item needs its own result approval. The owner's approval of the
  parent does not cover it.
- Finishing a sub-item never finishes or approves its parent.

## 11. Standing merge instruction

A merge normally needs the owner's yes to that merge. A standing merge
instruction replaces that yes only when all of these hold:

- [ ] `DECISIONS.md` records it as the owner's decision (the project's
      `AGENTS.md` may point at it);
- [ ] an `acceptance-checker` that did not build the change reported no
      blocking issue on that exact head commit;
- [ ] every check passes on that head;
- [ ] the work item does not say its merge needs the owner's approval (an
      item that says so overrides the instruction).

Without an independent check the instruction does not apply: ask the owner.
A new commit after the check means a new check on the new head.

## 12. When an approve command refuses

- Show the owner the command's error in plain words. Never work around it by
  editing the record, the design text, or a header field.
- The error names what is missing (for example the Agreed goal still holds
  the template text). Fix that, then run the same command again.
- Exit code 2 means a refused gate: the record is unchanged.

# Closing a work item

The detail behind each `work-finish` step: the pull request and merge, a
merge with no remote, deployment, the requirements baseline, sub-items,
memory, leftover worktrees, Done, and cancel.

## Contents

1. Before anything ships
2. Commit, push, and the pull request (stage 12)
3. Merging
4. No remote: the local merge
5. Deployment (stage 13)
6. Requirements baseline (stage 14)
7. Sub-items
8. Memory and the current focus
9. Leftover worktrees and branches
10. Done
11. Cancel

## 1. Before anything ships

- The result approval is recorded (`toolkit work show <id>` shows
  `result_approved`), or the owner said "ship it" or "mark it done" after he
  saw the result, the gaps, and the evidence. Record that with his words
  (`approvals.md`, "Result approval").
- Never describe an unverified result as complete.
- Done means the owner accepted the result. Cancelled means the work stopped
  without it.
- Stages that do not apply are skipped. Work with no repository change has no
  pull request; work with no deployment has no deployment stage. A skipped
  stage gets one history note saying so, so `toolkit work finish` has a
  record of it.

## 2. Commit, push, and the pull request (stage 12)

- Commit the item's files on its branch, staged by name
  (`claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, for example `claude/wi-007-csv-export`).
  No `Co-Authored-By` line naming an AI and no "Generated with" line.
- Push the branch. Never force-push.
- Write the pull request title and description in plain words: what changed,
  why, how it was checked, and the item id. Run the description through the
  `unslop` skill, because other people read it. No line crediting an AI.
- Set the stage:
  `toolkit work set <id> --stage 12-pr-and-push`
- In Codex, every Git write here needs the owner's approval and escalated
  permissions (`git-rules.md`).

## 3. Merging

Merge only through `merge-and-clean-up`, and only when one of these holds:

- the owner said yes to this merge; or
- a standing merge instruction applies (`approvals.md`, "Standing merge
  instruction"): it is recorded in `DECISIONS.md`, an `acceptance-checker`
  that did not build the change found no blocking issue on that exact head
  commit, and every check passes.

A work item that says its merge needs the owner's approval overrides a
standing instruction. Without an independent check, the standing instruction
does not apply: ask the owner.

A merge that stops on a conflict: resolve it and commit with a message you
write (`git commit -m 'Merge <branch>: <what it brings>'`). Never
`git commit --no-edit`: it keeps Git's "# Conflicts:" lines in the message.

## 4. No remote: the local merge

`git remote` prints nothing: the project has no remote. There is no push and
no pull request, and `git fetch` is never run.

- [ ] The same approval as a merge applies (section 3).
- [ ] The merge-safety check (`git-rules.md`, "The merge-safety check"):
      list the files the merge brings in, and the primary checkout's
      uncommitted files. A file in both lists: stop, name exactly those
      files, and let the owner decide.
      `git diff --name-only <default branch>...<branch>`
      `git -C <primary checkout> status --porcelain`
- [ ] In the main checkout, on the default branch:
      `git merge --ff-only <branch>`
- [ ] The fast-forward fails when the default branch moved on after the
      item's branch was made (for example another item's local merge). Then,
      in the item's worktree: `git merge <default branch>`, run the item's
      checks again (under a standing merge instruction the
      `acceptance-checker` checks the new head), run the merge-safety check
      again, and run the fast-forward again.
- [ ] Set the stage anyway and record it, with the real name of the default
      branch in the note:
      `toolkit work set <id> --stage 12-pr-and-push`
      `toolkit work history <id> --note 'No remote: merged locally into <default branch>.' --effect 'No pull request; no deployment.'`

## 5. Deployment (stage 13)

Only when the result must be put somewhere beyond the default branch.

`toolkit work set <id> --stage 13-deployment`

Salesforce projects, in order:

- [ ] `sf-component-tracker` is current, and the item's folder
      `delivery/deployment/<work-item-id>-<short-name>/` holds its
      `package.xml`, `destructiveChanges.xml` when something is removed,
      `manual-steps.md`, and `DEPLOYMENT-RECORD.md`.
- [ ] `sf-deploy-check` finds nothing that would ship too early.
- [ ] A validate against the sandbox. It needs no yes, in both hosts.
- [ ] A sandbox deploy, when the item needs one: in Claude Code, only after
      the owner's yes for that deploy, in this chat.
- [ ] In Codex, the owner runs every sandbox deploy and sandbox data change,
      including `sf apex run` against a sandbox. Hand him the exact command
      with its `-o <sandbox>`; do not run it yourself, even after his yes.
- [ ] Run each `sf` command directly, never from a script or file you wrote,
      so the guard sees it (`salesforce-org-safety.md`).
- [ ] A DevOps Center pipeline deploy (`sf project deploy pipeline start`,
      `quick`, `resume`, or `validate`) goes to the owner: the command does
      not name the org it reaches, and that org can be production.
- [ ] A production deploy is handed to the owner: the exact command, what it
      deploys, and what to check afterwards. Agents never run it.
- [ ] Production data changes go through `sf-data-change`, which builds the
      owner's package. The owner runs it.
- [ ] A release of several items uses a copy of
      `delivery/deployment/release-cutover-template/`.

Record the owner's report of the deploy in a history note.

## 6. Requirements baseline (stage 14)

`toolkit work set <id> --stage 14-spec-update`

- The work item held the proposed requirements while the work was in
  progress. After delivery and approval, copy the delivered rules into the
  area's file in `requirements/`. Read `requirements/AGENTS.md` first.
- Each business area has one folder holding one maintained file. A new area:
  copy `requirements/system-area-template/` to a folder named for the area,
  then name the copied `AREA-TEMPLATE.md` for the area, for example
  `requirements/billing/BILLING.md`. Fill it as its guide says and delete the
  guide. Leave `system-area-template/` unchanged for the next area.
- Rules that apply across areas go in `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md`.
- Copy only behavior that was delivered and approved. Behavior that was
  approved but not delivered is never written as shipped.
- Link the work item id from the area file when it explains a requirement,
  and add a line to its Change history. Do not copy task history there.
- When the change altered the verified structure of the system, also update
  the area's file in `system-guide/` (a new area is a copy of
  `system-guide/AREA-TEMPLATE.md` named for the area, for example
  `system-guide/billing.md`), with the observed facts and the date checked.
- Save these files with the `publish-docs` skill. It commits them from its own
  worktree and pushes them; with no remote it commits them on the default
  branch locally and says "No remote: committed locally".
- Confirm the item links to the requirements, decisions, and code that
  actually exist. Do not create missing documents only to complete a
  checklist.

## 7. Sub-items

- List the open sub-items before finishing a parent:
  `toolkit work list --tree`
- Each one is finished or cancelled on its own (with its own approval or
  reason), or moved when the owner asks (`work-organize`).
- A parent with open sub-items is finished only when the owner says so. Then
  `toolkit work finish` needs `--allow-open-sub-items` (without it the
  command refuses with exit code 2), and a history note quotes his words.
- Finishing a sub-item never finishes or approves its parent.
- Cancelling a parent: ask what happens to each open sub-item (cancel it,
  move it to the top level, or move it under another item). Never cancel
  them without asking.

## 8. Memory and the current focus

- At most one `event` memory through `memory-save`, only when the episode will
  matter later, for example a costly fix or a surprising platform limit.
- Take the item off the current focus "Now" list, replace a "Next session
  starts with" line that names it, and update the "Last updated" line
  (`current-focus.md`). The focus names work item ids, never their status.

## 9. Leftover worktrees and branches

- List the item's worktrees and branches, with its id prefix in lower case:
  `git worktree list`
  `git branch --list '*wi-007*'`
- Compare each with the default branch. Offer to remove the ones already
  delivered. Remove one only with the owner's yes, and never one that holds
  uncommitted work: `git worktree remove <folder>`, then
  `git branch -d <branch>`. A merged pull request's branch and worktree are
  removed by `merge-and-clean-up`.
- `git status` in the main checkout must show none of the item's files
  uncommitted.

## 10. Done

Run the Done checklist in `approvals.md` first. Then:

- Before the finish command: set each Roadmap phase the item completed to
  Done, and in Overview bring Related items up to date (which sub-items
  delivered what, and anything left to another item), set Current position to
  "Done on <date>: <evidence>", and set Blockers to "None.". A Done item that
  still names a deleted branch or a merge waiting for approval misleads the
  next reader.
- `toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>'`.
  The evidence names the test result, the pull request or commit, or what
  the owner saw. The command sets Next action to "None. Finished." and Notes >
  Resume here to "Finished on <date>. Nothing to resume.", and prints a note
  when stages 12 to 14 left no record or a Roadmap phase is not Done. Answer
  each note it prints.
- The finish command then backs up `.work-items/` and `.memory/` (and
  Hindsight memory) to the owner's backup folder, and prints one line about
  it. Read that line:
  - "Backed up ... to <folder>": say it in one line in the reply.
  - "No backup folder is set ...": ask the owner for a folder outside the
    project, as the one question of the reply. After his answer:
    `toolkit config set backup.dir <folder>` (`none` when he wants no
    backup).
  - A line with "failed" or "Tell the owner": tell him that line as it is.
    The item is still Done; only the backup is missing.
- Repository work: say whether the work reached the default branch.
- Leave the folder or card where it is. Moving or archiving happens only on
  the owner's request, through `work-organize`.
- End the reply with the one question for the owner (the merge, the deploy, a
  leftover branch, the backup folder), or the exact words that continue
  ("Tell me the next thing to build.").

## 11. Cancel

- `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`. The reason is his
  words, not a summary.
- Ask about each open sub-item first (section 7).
- Cancelling keeps the record. Nothing is deleted.

# Running `toolkit` commands

Purpose: how to run a `toolkit` command in Claude Code and in Codex, how to
pass text in one, and what each exit code means. Every skill that runs a
`toolkit` command follows this file.

## Contents

- Running toolkit commands
- Text in a command
- Exit codes
- Reporting a save
- Reading output and updating what you read
- Right and wrong examples

## Running toolkit commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command,
  in both hosts. Do not join it to another command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe,
  and do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a loop, or a script. This holds for read
  commands too: `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two
  commands, run one after the other.
- Why, in Codex: the project's command rule (`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules`)
  runs a `toolkit` command outside the sandbox only when it is the whole
  command. A `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion, the
  local Hindsight server, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and
  `.memory/` from a worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong
  cause.
- The one thing a Claude Code command may carry is its own text on standard
  input (`--set-file -` with a quoted heredoc; "Text in a command", below).
- Five commands ask the owner first, in both hosts, because they are hard or
  impossible to undo: `toolkit machine-setup`, `toolkit memory delete`,
  `toolkit memory import`, `toolkit import`, and
  `toolkit hindsight service install` or `start`. Get his yes in the reply
  before you run one. The host then asks him to confirm the command (Claude
  Code: a permission prompt; Codex: an approval). That prompt is expected, not
  an error.
- In Codex, run each of those five alone, with `sandbox_permissions` set to
  `require_escalated` and a one-line reason. The approval alone keeps the
  command inside the sandbox, where it fails: `toolkit memory delete` cannot
  reach Hindsight or Notion, `toolkit machine-setup` cannot write `~/.codex`
  or `~/.local/bin`, `toolkit hindsight service install` cannot write
  `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, and `toolkit import` from a worktree cannot write
  the main checkout.
- Write `--json` and `--host` after the command words
  (`toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved --json`). The toolkit refuses
  those five commands when a flag comes first, because the ask-first rules
  would not match them.
- Never change a work item or a memory record with a script or a shell write
  (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`, `tee`, `cp`). Use the `toolkit` command
  that owns it. The hooks refuse the shell write, so it only wastes a step.
- `toolkit help <command>` prints every option of one command.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still reports success. So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Never use double quotes for text.
- **An apostrophe inside single quotes:**
  - Claude Code: write it as `'\''`, for example
    `--note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`.
  - Codex: write it as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the text.
    Never `'\''` in Codex: the command rule does not match that form, so the
    command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can drop the
    backslash, which leaves a quote that is never closed.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere.
  Claude Code refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary file there
  could never be deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line
  holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --set-file - <<'EOF'
  <the whole section text>
  EOF
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text:
  1. Make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d`. Its name is
     unique, so two sessions or two projects never share a file.
  2. Write the file in it with the file edit tool (`apply_patch`).
  3. Run the `toolkit` command alone, with the file's full path.
  4. Delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds
     (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner anything.

  Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
  ```

- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`. Every
  project starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this
  item.
- Never leave a draft file inside `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. A second
  `DESIGN.md`-shaped file there confuses the design lookup, and a stray note
  in `.memory/` is read as a memory.

## Exit codes

`toolkit help work` prints them as: "0 ok, 1 error, 2 validation failure or a
refused gate, 3 not supported for this tracker, 4 not a toolkit project."
`toolkit help memory` uses the same numbers: "1 error or not found, 2 refused
(a rule or a stale --expect), 3 not supported by this backend".

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | Done. | Read back what you wrote before you report it as saved ("Reporting a save", below). A "Note:" line in the output still needs action: report it to the owner, or do what it says. |
| `1` | Error, or the record was not found. | Read the message. It names the cause and usually the fix. Do not run the same command again unchanged. |
| `2` | Validation failure, a refused gate, or a stale `--expect`. | Fix what the message names and run the command again. A refused gate means an approval is missing: ask the owner for it. Never work around a refusal. |
| `3` | Not supported for this tracker or memory backend. | For a GitHub or Jira tracker, the message prints the path of the written instructions for that tracker. Follow them to make the same change on the issue. |
| `4` | Not a Toolkit V2 project. | Skip every work item and memory step and say so in one line. To set the project up, open the `project-setup` skill. |

`toolkit: command not found` means this computer cannot reach the command.
The `project-setup` skill fixes that.

## Reporting a save

- Save each settled answer before moving on, then read it back. A command
  that exits `0` is not proof by itself.
- A write failed: lead the reply with "Not saved". Name what was not saved
  and where it should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- "Saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first part that differs. Lead the
  reply with "Saved but not verified", say which part, and read the record
  back to judge it.

## Reading output and updating what you read

- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field, for example
  a record's `version`.
- `--expect <version>` tells the command which version of a record you read.
  The command refuses the save (exit `2`) when the record changed since then,
  so you never overwrite a newer edit. Read it again, merge, and save with the
  new version. `toolkit memory focus`, `toolkit memory glossary`, and
  `toolkit memory save` take it. `--expect absent` says it must not exist
  yet: a new record, or a project with no focus yet.

## Right and wrong examples

1. Two reads.
   - Wrong: `toolkit work list && toolkit work show WI-004`
   - Right: `toolkit work list`, then, as a second command,
     `toolkit work show WI-004`.
2. A history note that quotes the owner, with an apostrophe in his words.
   - Wrong: ``toolkit work history WI-004 --note "Owner said: it's ready, `ship it`"``
     (double quotes: the shell runs the words between the backticks as a
     command and saves its output in their place).
   - Right in Claude Code:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`
   - Right in Codex:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it’s ready, ship it"'`
   - The prefix is `Owner said:`, which has no apostrophe to escape.
3. Section text in Codex.
   - Wrong: `cat > /tmp/overview.md <<'EOF' ... EOF && toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --set-file /tmp/overview.md`
     (one shell command, a heredoc, and a fixed file name).
   - Right: `toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'`
4. A change to a work item's header.
   - Wrong: `sed -i '' 's/^stage: .*/stage: 04-solution-design/' .work-items/WI-004/WORK-ITEM.md`
   - Right: `toolkit work set WI-004 --stage 04-solution-design --note '<why>'`
5. Toolkit commands from a script.
   - Wrong: `for id in WI-001 WI-002; do toolkit work show $id; done`
   - Right: `toolkit work show WI-001`, then `toolkit work show WI-002`, each
     as its own command.

# Git rules for Toolkit V2 skills

Purpose: the Git rules every Toolkit V2 skill follows when it makes a branch,
commits, merges, pushes, or removes a worktree, in Claude Code and in Codex.

## Contents

- Look before the first Git write
- Branch and worktree names for a work item
- Staging and committing
- No AI credit
- The Git-ignored toolkit folders
- A project with no remote
- The merge-safety check
- A merge that stops on a conflict
- Git writes in Codex
- Checklist: one commit
- Examples

## Look before the first Git write

Other sessions may work in the same repository at the same time. Before the
first Git write in a session, run each of these on its own:

```text
git worktree list
git status
git remote
```

- `git remote` prints nothing: the project has no remote. Read "A project
  with no remote" below before any fetch, pull, push, or pull request.
- An unknown worktree, a branch that moved, or a change this session did not
  make means another session is working. Do not change it. Tell the owner.
- The shared primary checkout is the first entry `git worktree list` prints.
  In it, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never commit, push, rebase, or delete another session's branch, and never
  commit its uncommitted changes, even when they look finished.

## Branch and worktree names for a work item

A work item's code work happens in its own worktree, on its own branch.

| Part | Form | Example for `WI-007`, "CSV export" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branch | `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` | `claude/wi-007-csv-export` |
| Worktree folder | `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` | `.claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export` |

- `<prefix>` is the item's own id prefix in lower case: `wi` for `WI-007`,
  `tv2` for `TV2-007`, `acme` for `ACME-007`.
- The session briefing and `merge-and-clean-up` find the item from the id in
  the branch name. A branch named `wi-001-<slug>` for item `TV2-001` is not
  linked to that item.
- Make both with one command:

  ```text
  git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export
  ```

- Build on the item's branch, never on the default branch.

## Staging and committing

- Stage each path by name. Never run `git add -A`, `git add .`, or
  `git commit -a`: in a shared checkout they take other sessions' files.
- Read the staged file list, then the full staged diff, before the commit.
  Unstage any file this session did not write.

  ```text
  git diff --cached --name-status
  git diff --cached
  ```

- Write a plain commit message that says what changed, in one line when one
  line is enough.

## No AI credit

Nothing committed or published names an AI as an author or a helper:

- no `Co-Authored-By:` line naming an AI (a line naming a real person is
  allowed);
- no "Generated with" line;
- no AI credit in a pull request title or description, a code comment, a file
  header, or release notes.

The pre-tool hook refuses a commit or pull request command that carries such
a line. When it refuses, change the wording. Never commit another way to get
past it.

## The Git-ignored toolkit folders

`.work-items/` and `.memory/` are Git-ignored and live in the main checkout.

- Never commit them, and never force them in with `git add -f`. The hook
  refuses it.
- Never run `git clean -x` or `git clean -X` in the main checkout. It deletes
  both folders, and Git cannot bring them back. The hook refuses it.
- They change only through `toolkit work` and `toolkit memory` commands.
- Their backup is automatic: `toolkit work finish` and the handoff copy them
  to the owner's backup folder (`toolkit handoff-backup` does the same on
  request). `toolkit export --to <folder>` makes a one-off copy.

## A project with no remote

`git remote` prints nothing.

- Never run `git fetch`, `git pull`, or `git push`. A fetch that fails or is
  refused is not a blocker: never report it as one, and never write it into a
  work item.
- There is no pull request. `work-finish` merges the item's branch into the
  default branch locally, after the same approval a pull request merge needs,
  from the main checkout:

  ```text
  git merge --ff-only claude/wi-007-csv-export
  ```

  Then it adds the history note "No remote: merged locally into
  <default branch>."
- The fast-forward fails when the default branch moved on after the item's
  branch was made (for example another item's local merge). Merge the default
  branch into the item's branch in the item's worktree (`git merge main`, with
  the real default branch name), run the item's checks again, then run the
  fast-forward again.
- Documents are committed on the local default branch. `publish-docs` does
  this by itself.
- `merge-and-clean-up`, `pull-latest`, and `reset-to-remote` have nothing to
  do. Say so in one line.

## The merge-safety check

Before any merge into the default branch, check that it cannot overwrite
another session's uncommitted work in the primary checkout. With a remote,
fetch first so the comparison uses the remote's default branch.

```text
git diff --name-only main...claude/wi-007-csv-export
git -C <primary checkout> status --porcelain
```

Use the real default branch name, and `origin/<default branch>` when there is
a remote. A file in both lists: stop, name exactly those files, and let the
owner decide whether to commit, stash, or wait. Never touch the primary
checkout's changes yourself.

## A merge that stops on a conflict

1. Read both sides of each conflicting file. When the right result is not
   clear from the two sides, stop and ask the owner.
2. Stage each resolved file by name.
3. Commit with a message you write:

   ```text
   git commit -m 'Merge main into claude/wi-007-csv-export: keep both export formats'
   ```

Never run `git commit --no-edit` after a conflict: it keeps Git's
"# Conflicts:" lines in the message.

## Git writes in Codex

Codex's sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only. Every command that writes `.git/`
fails inside it: `git add`, `commit`, `merge`, `fetch`, `pull`, `push`,
`switch`, `checkout`, `restore`, `rm`, `mv`, `stash`, `cherry-pick`,
`revert`, `rebase`, `reset`, `update-ref`, `git worktree add`, `remove`,
`move`, `prune`, and `repair`, and `git branch -d`, `-D`, `-m`, `-c`, and
`-f`. The project's
`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` makes Codex ask the owner before each one. A `gh`
call that needs the network is also refused inside the sandbox.

Reading commands (`git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`,
`git branch --list`, `git worktree list`) run inside the sandbox as usual.

For each Git write in Codex:

- [ ] Run the Git command alone, as its own command: not joined to another
      command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and not from a script.
- [ ] Say in one line what the command does, before Codex asks the owner.
- [ ] Ask for escalated permissions: set `sandbox_permissions` to
      `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason that says what the command
      does ("Create the worktree for WI-002 on its own branch."). An approval
      without escalation still runs the command inside the sandbox, where it
      fails on `.git/index.lock`.
- [ ] Codex refused it without asking ("approval required by policy", or
      "AskForApproval is set to Never"): this session cannot ask. Stop that
      step, show the owner the exact command, and ask him to approve it in an
      interactive session or run it in a terminal. Set the work item waiting
      on the owner. It is not an outside blocker.

Never work around a refusal: no nested `git clone` of the project, no copy of
`.git/`, no script that runs Git for you, and no building on the default
branch instead of the item's branch. The `publish-docs` script is not such a
script: it is that skill's own tool. Run it alone with escalated permissions,
like any other Git write.

## Checklist: one commit

```text
- [ ] In the right worktree, on the right branch (git branch --show-current)
- [ ] Each path staged by name
- [ ] Staged list read: only this session's files, no .work-items/ or .memory/
- [ ] Full staged diff read
- [ ] Plain message with no AI credit line
- [ ] Codex: each Git command run alone, with escalated permissions
```

## Examples

Right: stage by name, read the list, commit.

```text
git add src/export.js tests/export.test.js
git diff --cached --name-status
git commit -m 'Add CSV export for invoices'
```

Wrong: `git add -A && git commit -m 'wip'`. It stages other sessions' files,
and in Codex the joined command runs inside the sandbox and fails.

Wrong: a message whose last line is a `Co-Authored-By:` trailer naming an AI
model. The hook refuses it. Remove the line and commit again.

Right, no remote: after the owner approves the result and the merge,

```text
git merge --ff-only claude/wi-007-csv-export
```

run from the main checkout, then the history note "No remote: merged locally
into main."

Right, Codex: `git commit -m 'Add CSV export for invoices'` run alone, with
`sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated` and the reason "Commit the
CSV export files for WI-007 on its branch."

9. Backup and restore

## 1. Where the items live

- `.work-items/` sits in the project's main checkout. It is Git-ignored and
  shared by every worktree, so every session sees the same items.
- Never commit `.work-items/`. Git does not back it up; the toolkit's
  automatic backup does (section 9).
- `toolkit config get tracker.type` prints `local` for this tracker.
- The project's own rule for this tracker is
  `.claude/rules/work-item-folders.md`.

## 2. An item is its id, not its path

- An item is a folder that holds `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` once it has
  a design. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is its identity. The
  folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by id everywhere, never by path.
- Find an item's files only with:
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next id under a
  lock, so parallel sessions never pick the same one. Ids are never reused.

## 3. Sub-items, groups, and the archive

- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item. Its
  `parent` follows its location.
- A plain folder with no record in it is a group. A group changes no parent.
  A sub-item cannot also sit in a group.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing,
  the dashboard, and `toolkit work next`. Archiving is not cancelling.
- Move items only when the owner asks:
  `toolkit work move <id> --under <parent-id>`
  `toolkit work move <id> --under <group>`
  `toolkit work move <id> --under archive`
  `toolkit work move <id> --under root`
- A move carries every nested item with it.

## 4. What the tracker ignores

- `work-item-template/` (the template the CLI copies);
- any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`;
- any record whose title is still `<Work item title>` (an unused template
  copy).

## 5. Generated and state files

- `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md`: the board as a file, rebuilt by every
  `toolkit work` write and by `toolkit work sync`.
- `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`: the id-to-path map and the highest id
  used.

Never edit either by hand or from the shell. The pre-tool hook refuses it.
"Show the board" means: summarize `DASHBOARD.md`.

## 6. What `toolkit work sync` does by itself

The session-start hook, the prompt hook, and every `toolkit work` command run
a sync. It rescans `.work-items/` and:

- follows a folder or file the owner moved or renamed, by the record's `id`;
- sets `parent` from the new location when a folder was nested inside another
  item's folder, or moved out of one;
- adopts a record with no id (a template copy with a real title): gives it
  the next free id and reports it;
- renumbers the newer of two records that share an id, and reports both;
- writes one Recent History row on each item the owner moved or renamed
  ("Moved by hand: <old path> -> <new path>", "Folder renamed by hand: ..."),
  and on the parents a sub-item left and joined ("Sub-item WI-7 moved out by
  hand", "Sub-item WI-7 moved here by hand");
- rebuilds `DASHBOARD.md`.

Every change is reported: in the session briefing under "Changes found in the
tracker", and by the next `toolkit work` command. Tell the owner each one in
one line before other work. Open `work-organize` for anything the report
calls missing or duplicated.

## 7. Worktrees and the item

- An item's code work happens in its own worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` on branch
  `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`. `<prefix>` is the item's id prefix in
  lower case: `wi` for `WI-007`, `tv2` for `TV2-007`.
- `toolkit work show <id>` prints the exact branch and folder to use.
- The briefing and `toolkit work next` tie a worktree to its item by the id in
  the branch name. A branch named `wi-001-...` is not linked to `TV2-001`.
- From a worktree, `toolkit work` still reads the main checkout's
  `.work-items/`.

## 8. Editing a record

- Prefer `toolkit work edit <id> --section '<heading>'`.
- Body text may also be changed with the file edit tool; the post-tool hook
  checks the record after each edit and reports problems.
- Header fields change only through `toolkit work set`, `approve`, `design`,
  `move`, `finish`, and `cancel`. A file edit that changes them is refused.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

## 9. Backup and restore

- The owner's backup folder is the `backup.dir` setting. Setup asks for it.
  `toolkit config get backup.dir`
- With it set, these back up `.work-items/` and `.memory/` (and Hindsight
  memory) to `<backup.dir>/<project key>-<YYYY-MM-DD>/` by themselves, and
  each prints one line about it:
  - `toolkit work finish`;
  - `toolkit handoff-backup`, the last step of the `handoff` skill;
  - the session start, when the last backup on this computer is more than a
    day old (`.work-items/` and `.memory/` only).
- Read that line. "Backed up ..." is done. "No backup folder is set ..."
  means: ask the owner for a folder outside the project, then
  `toolkit config set backup.dir <folder>` (`none` when he wants no backup).
  A line with "failed" or "Tell the owner" goes to him as it is; the work
  itself is saved.
- `toolkit export --to <folder>` is the backup by hand, to a new folder
  outside the project.
- `toolkit doctor` warns when no backup folder is set, when it cannot be
  reached, and when the last backup is more than a day old. When the owner
  chose `none`, it only notes a last export more than 7 days old.
- A restore runs only when the owner asks. Before it, back up the current
  state to a new folder, so the restore can be undone. Then a dry run, then
  the real run after his yes. Both hosts ask the owner to allow every
  `toolkit import` command, the dry run too, so tell him the prompt is
  coming.
  `toolkit import --from <folder> --dry-run`
  `toolkit import --from <folder>`
- A file that differs is a conflict, and then nothing is written unless
  `--replace` is given. Use `--replace` only after the owner's yes to the
  exact files the dry run named.
- The full restore order, with memory and a new computer, is in the
  `project-setup` skill. Open it when the owner asks for a restore.
